title: {{NAME}} and the Kingdom Under the Storm
moral: Bravery is not the absence of fear, but the decision to act while still afraid, for something that matters more than the fear.

pages.content: The Kingdom of Amberveil had three famous things: the best honey in the world, a princess with exceptional strategic instincts, and a catastrophic storm that arrived every seven years and lasted, without apology, for three days. The storm was famous too, in the way that difficult things become famous: through repetition and endurance. {{NAME}} arrived at Amberveil's borders as the sky turned the specific shade of yellow-green that precedes serious weather, a colour that has no name but does not need one, because everyone who sees it understands immediately. He had been tracking the storm for a week. The palace at Amberveil's centre was the highest structure in the region, and its tower beacons served as guidance for every animal in the lowland plains when the floods came. If the beacons went out, the animals would lose their way. The beacons ran on a crystal-and-oil system. {{NAME}} had the crystal in his pocket. What he did not yet know was what had already begun inside the palace walls.

pages.content: Princess Tova was in the beacon tower when {{NAME}} arrived, and she was not waiting to be rescued. She had assessed the beacon system, identified the precise location of the crystal failure three days before {{NAME}} had even known there was a problem, and despatched six separate missions to find a replacement. All six had failed or not returned. She was now on her third attempt to repurpose the existing oil system to produce enough light to serve as a beacon on its own, which was possible in theory and very much not working in practice. She looked up when {{NAME}} arrived at the tower door, registered the crystal in his hand with the expression of someone revising their opinion of the day, and said, with great precision: good, that is the correct crystal, put it here. He put it there. The system came online. Outside, the storm arrived. It hit the palace like a decision that had been made far away and could not now be unmade, all at once, with full commitment.

pages.content: The beacons burned bright above the storm-beaten palace, and the animals of the lowland plains followed them as they had always done, the deer moving in tight groups, the foxes running the ridge, the slower animals guided by the faster ones in those ancient, unspoken arrangements that exist between creatures who have survived many storms together. But the storm's eastern arm had cut a new channel through a gully {{NAME}} knew, and he could see from the tower window that the deer herd's usual route was already flooding. He was in the air before Tova had finished saying his name. The flight through the storm was brutal, wind hitting him from three angles at once, rain needling at every exposed surface, lightning close enough to feel as heat. He found the deer at the edge of the flooded gully, twelve of them, the largest standing at the front facing the water with the particular posture of an animal calculating odds and not liking the result. {{NAME}} landed in front of them, lit by his own bronze glow, and pointed the direction he had already scouted on the way down: a higher path, wider and dry, invisible from ground level. The largest deer considered this for three seconds and then moved.

pages.content: He was on his third flight, guiding the last group of river otters to the high bank, when the storm threw something he had not expected: a bolt of lightning struck the palace tower's east spire at precisely the wrong angle and the beacon above the tower swung wide on its mounting, its light angling sideways into nothing instead of outward across the plains. {{NAME}} felt it. From six hundred metres up in the dark and rain, he saw the beacon veer and he understood immediately what it meant for the animals still moving in the plains below. He could go back and fix it. Or he could stay with the otters, who were frightened and needed a guide for the remaining five minutes to safety. He could not do both. He looked at the otters. He looked at the beacon. He shouted to Tova on the wind, no words, just a direction, trusting her to understand. She did. He saw her silhouette on the spire as he led the otters the last of the way, her hands on the mounting, leaning into the storm with complete, focused calm. The beacon swung back. The plains blazed with light. Neither of them had been certain the other would be enough. Both of them had trusted it anyway.

pages.content: The storm lasted three days, as advertised, and then departed with the same completeness with which it had arrived. The plains were muddy and rearranged and full of the smell of freshly turned earth and new beginnings. Every animal was accounted for. The beacons had burned throughout. {{NAME}} sat on the palace steps in the pale, washed-clean light of the morning after, his scarlet suit still damp at the seams, his bronze cape spread on the step below him to dry. Tova sat beside him, her notes in her lap, already annotating the storm's behaviour for the records she kept on all seven-year events. The animals were returning to the plain below in loose, unhurried groups, pausing at the water that had collected in the hollows to drink. The largest deer, the one who had moved first, stopped at the base of the palace steps and looked up, long and direct, and then walked on. {{NAME}}'s eyes were heavy and his muscles were the particular kind of tired that lives deeper than tired. He leaned back on the warm stone and the sun found his face. He was asleep before Tova had finished her second annotation, his breathing slow and even. In the valley below, the honey bees were already returning to work, and the season that followed the great storm, as everyone in Amberveil knew, was always the sweetest.
